data.name: Lipase
data.description: Lipase is an enzyme made mainly by your pancreas. Its job is to help your body break down fats in the food you eat. Think of it as a “fat cutter” — it turns big fat molecules into smaller pieces so your body can absorb and use them. Doctors usually check your lipase levels to see if your pancreas is inflamed or irritated. This condition is called pancreatitis. A high lipase level can be a sign something's wrong with the pancreas.

data.name: ADMA/SDMA
data.description: This panel measures Asymmetric Dimethylarginine (ADMA) and Symmetric Dimethylarginine (SDMA)—two key markers of vascular health, nitric oxide metabolism, and kidney function. ADMA reflects endothelial dysfunction and impaired nitric oxide production (linked to blood pressure, inflammation, and aging), while SDMA is a sensitive indicator of kidney filtration efficiency. Together, they provide early insight into cardiovascular risk, renal stress, and metabolic resilience, often before more common markers show problems.

data.name: C-Reactive Protein (CRP)
data.description: CRP is an acute phase reactant, which can be used as a test for inflammatory diseases, infections, and neoplastic diseases. Progressive increases correlate with increases of inflammation/injury. CRP is a more sensitive, rapidly responding indicator than ESR. CRP may be used to detect early postoperative wound infection and to follow therapeutic response to anti-inflammatory agents. Recent reports have indicated that a highly sensitive version of the CRP assay may be used as an additional indicator for susceptibility to cardiac disease.

data.name: Lipid Panel With (ApoB), GlycA, and (DRI)
data.description: This expanded lipid panel combines traditional cholesterol markers (Total Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, VLDL, Triglycerides) with ApoB (the actual number of atherogenic particles), GlycA (chronic inflammation marker), and the DRI (Disease Risk Index)—a composite score evaluating your long-term cardiometabolic risk. This advanced panel gives a clearer picture of how lipids, inflammation, and particle count interact to influence cardiovascular health, longevity, and metabolic resilience.

labOptions.biomarkerName: Lipid Panel With (ApoB), GlycA, and (DRI) - LabCorp

data.name: Fructosamine
data.description: Fructosamine gives you a snapshot of your average blood sugar over the past 2–3 weeks. It reflects how much glucose has been sticking to your blood proteins — sort of like a shorter-term version of HbA1c. It’s super useful if you’re actively tweaking your diet, exercise, or supplements and want quicker feedback than waiting 3 months for an A1c shift.

data.name: Zinc
data.description: Zinc is a critical trace mineral that supports testosterone production, immune function, recovery, energy metabolism, and even mental clarity. You burn through it faster with intense training, stress, or inflammation. It’s not stored in the body, so levels can dip without obvious symptoms at first — think of it like a daily-use resource for high-performance living.

data.name: Vitamin B12
data.description: Vitamin B12 is essential for energy production, red blood cell formation, brain function, and methylation. It helps convert food into energy and supports your nervous system. Low B12 can cause fatigue, brain fog, poor memory, mood issues, and even nerve problems. Total B12 doesn’t always reflect functional use—so levels should ideally be well above the deficiency cutoff.

data.name: HCG (pregnancy test) Ql
data.description: This test measures the β-subunit of human chorionic gonadotropin (β-hCG) in the blood. hCG is a hormone normally produced by the placenta during pregnancy, but trace amounts can be found in non-pregnant individuals. In healthy men and non-pregnant women, levels are typically undetectable or below 5 mIU/mL. Elevated results may indicate pregnancy, recent pregnancy, or—less commonly—certain tumors (such as germ-cell or trophoblastic types). Interpretation depends on clinical context and should always be correlated with other findings.

data.name: Thyroid Peroxidase (TPO Antibodies)
data.description: TPO antibodies show whether your immune system is mistakenly attacking your thyroid. Elevated levels are a red flag for autoimmune thyroid conditions like Hashimoto’s or Graves’. Even if your thyroid hormones look “normal,” rising TPO suggests your body is laying the groundwork for future issues — often triggered by stress, infections, gut problems, or environmental toxins.

data.name: HbA1c
data.description: HbA1c reflects your average blood sugar over the past 2–3 months. It measures how much glucose has been sticking to your red blood cells. While fasting glucose shows how you're doing right now, HbA1c shows how you've been doing long-term. It's a strong indicator of insulin sensitivity, metabolic flexibility, and aging rate—and one of the best predictors of chronic disease risk when elevated.HbA1c reflects your average blood sugar over the past 2–3 months. It measures how much glucose has been sticking to your red blood cells. While fasting glucose shows how you're doing right now, HbA1c shows how you've been doing long-term. It's a strong indicator of insulin sensitivity, metabolic flexibility, and aging rate—and one of the best predictors of chronic disease risk when elevated.

data.name: Comp. Metabolic Panel (14)
data.description: The Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP-14) is a foundational blood test that measures 14 key markers related to electrolyte balance, kidney function, liver health, glucose control, and protein status. It provides a snapshot of how well your body is handling energy production, detoxification, hydration, and overall metabolic stability. Essential for tracking how your system is adapting to diet, training, stress, or recovery protocols.

data.name: Cortisol
data.description: Cortisol is your primary stress hormone — but it's not just about stress. It helps regulate energy, blood sugar, inflammation, and even your circadian rhythm. You want it high in the morning to feel alert and motivated, then gradually taper down by night. Too high for too long? Burnout, belly fat, and poor sleep. Too low? Fatigue, brain fog, low motivation.

data.name: Protein
data.description: Total Protein measures the combined levels of albumin and globulins in your blood—key players in immune function, nutrient transport, and healing. It reflects your body’s overall nutritional status, liver function, and ability to recover from stress or injury. Low protein may signal poor digestion, liver issues, or undernourishment, while high protein could point to inflammation or immune activation. A solid foundation marker for recovery, repair, and resilience.

data.name: Urate [Mass/Vol]
data.description: You ca think of uric acid as a natural waste product that builds up when your body processes certain foods and your own cells. It's like the "trash" that needs to be cleared out through your kidneys.

data.name: Anti-Mullerian Hormone
data.description: AMH is a snapshot of your ovarian reserve — the number of eggs you have left. Higher AMH means more follicles and usually stronger fertility potential, while lower AMH may suggest declining reserve or perimenopause. It’s also commonly elevated in PCOS. While AMH doesn’t tell you everything about fertility, it’s one of the most trusted early indicators of how your reproductive system is aging.

data.name: Aldosterone:Renin Ratio (panel)
data.description: This ratio helps you understand how your body is managing salt, water, and blood pressure. It compares two key hormones—aldosterone and renin—to see if your system is in balance or if something’s pushing it out of whack, like stress, poor sleep, or high sodium. Useful for spotting signs of adrenal or blood pressure issues before they become a problem.

data.name: Testosterone, Free and Total
data.description: Testosterone,Free and Total

data.name: Cystatin C with eGFR
data.description: This test measures Cystatin C, a sensitive marker of kidney filtration, alongside a calculated eGFR (estimated glomerular filtration rate) based on that value. Unlike creatinine, Cystatin C isn't influenced by muscle mass, making it more accurate for athletes, lean individuals, and early detection of kidney issues. Together, these values give a clearer picture of how well your body is filtering out waste, supporting detox, and maintaining long-term metabolic balance.

data.name: Glucose
data.description: Glucose tells you how much sugar is circulating in your blood after not eating. It’s one of the fastest, most accessible markers of metabolic health. Elevated fasting glucose is often the first sign of insulin resistance, poor carb tolerance, or chronic stress. If your glucose is consistently high, your body is working harder than it should to maintain homeostasis—even if you feel “fine.”

data.name: Progesterone
data.description: Progesterone is your body’s calm-down hormone — it helps regulate the menstrual cycle, supports pregnancy, improves sleep, balances mood, and counteracts estrogen. In women, levels spike after ovulation and drop before menstruation. Low levels can mean estrogen dominance, cycle irregularities, fertility issues, or poor sleep. In men, it plays a subtle but real role in libido, mood, and brain function, and helps modulate estrogen.

data.name: ABO Grouping and Rho(D) Typing
data.description: ABO Grouping and Rho(D) Typing

ABO Grouping and Rho(D) Typing - Quest

data.name: Urea nitrogen
data.description: Urea nitrogen is a byproduct of protein metabolism, processed in the liver and excreted by the kidneys. It reflects protein turnover, hydration status, and renal function. Low levels might indicate under-eating protein or liver issues, while high levels can result from dehydration, high protein intake, intense training, or impaired kidney function. BUN is most useful when paired with creatinine to assess filtration efficiency and nitrogen balance.

data.name: Selenium (Bld)
data.description: Selenium is a trace mineral that powers up thyroid function, antioxidant defense, and immune resilience. It helps convert T4 into active T3, and protects your cells from oxidative stress — especially in the brain, thyroid, and reproductive system. Even small deficiencies can impact energy, mood, fertility, and inflammation levels. But too much? That can backfire too — think of selenium like a precision tool, not a blunt instrument.

data.name: ApoB and ApoA1 + Ratio
data.description: This ratio compares the amount of “bad” lipoproteins (ApoB) to “good” ones (ApoA1). A lower ratio means you’ve got more protective particles clearing cholesterol and fewer particles that cause buildup. It’s one of the best predictors of cardiovascular risk.

data.name: Thyroid Stimulating Hormone (TSH)
data.description: TSH isn’t a thyroid hormone—it’s the control signal from your brain telling your thyroid to make more T3 and T4. Higher TSH usually means your brain is yelling at the thyroid to work harder. Lower TSH means your brain thinks the thyroid is doing fine or even overproducing.

data.name: Gamma Glutamyl Transferase (GGT)
data.description: GGT is an enzyme involved in glutathione metabolism and is highly sensitive to liver stress, toxin exposure, and oxidative damage. It rises early when the liver is under pressure—from alcohol, medications, environmental toxins, or chronic inflammation. GGT is one of the best early warning markers for detox overload, and it often elevates before ALT or AST. When paired with ferritin, it can also reflect oxidative stress burden and long-term disease risk.

data.name: Homocysteine
data.description: Homocysteine is a byproduct of methionine metabolism, and when it builds up, it becomes a pro-aging, pro-inflammatory compound. High levels are linked to cardiovascular disease, Alzheimer’s risk, blood vessel damage, and even fertility issues. It’s heavily influenced by your B-vitamin status — especially B6, B12, and folate. If you’re thinking about brain, heart, or longevity optimization, this is a quiet but powerful marker to watch.

data.name: T3 Uptake
data.description: T3 Uptake isn’t a direct measure of T3—it reflects how much thyroid-binding protein (mostly TBG) is available in your blood. High uptake means less binding protein (more free hormone available), and low uptake means more binding protein (less free hormone). It’s mainly used to help calculate Free Thyroxine Index (FTI) and to interpret T4 levels more accurately. Useful for spotting binding protein imbalances from estrogen, liver issues, or stress.

data.name: Transferrin
data.description:
Transferrin is your blood’s main iron transport protein — think of it like the Uber that picks up iron and takes it where it needs to go. When transferrin levels go up, your body is often trying to grab more iron. When levels drop, it might mean inflammation is blocking iron transport or your liver isn’t making enough.

This marker gives great context alongside serum iron, ferritin, and iron saturation to spot low iron, inflammation, or early liver issues.

data.name: LH
data.description: LH is a pituitary hormone that triggers testosterone production in men and ovulation in women. It’s part of the HPG axis and works closely with FSH. In men, low LH often means stress, suppressed pituitary function, or high estrogen feedback. In women, LH surges to trigger ovulation—chronic elevation may point to PCOS, while low levels can reflect hypothalamic amenorrhea. It's a high-leverage hormone for tracking fertility, hormonal balance, and endocrine health.

data.name: Testosterone Free & Total, LC/MS-MS, Uncapped
data.description:
This panel measures both total testosterone (all testosterone circulating in your blood) and free testosterone (the fraction not bound to proteins and available for your body to use). Free testosterone is often the best indicator of how much “active” testosterone your tissues can access.

Note: When processed through BioReference lab, this panel also includes a measurement of SHBG (sex hormone–binding globulin), which helps interpret free vs. bound testosterone more precisely.

Because this panel uses LC/MS-MS (liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry), it’s highly accurate even at low or very high levels. Unlike some common lab methods, it does not cap out at 1500 ng/dL, making it useful for tracking both deficiency and supraphysiological levels.
If you're optimizing performance, energy, libido, or tracking testosterone therapy, this panel gives you the real data that matters.

data.name: Sex Hormone Binding Globulin (SHGB)
data.description: SHBG is a transport protein that binds to sex hormones—mainly testosterone and estrogen—and controls how much is free vs. bound. High SHBG means less free testosterone is available (even if total T is normal). Low SHBG can increase free hormone, but may also signal insulin resistance, liver issues, or androgen excess. It’s a key marker for hormone bioavailability, and crucial for interpreting total vs. free T.

data.name: Pregnenolone
data.description: Pregnenolone is the master hormone precursor—the raw material your body uses to make DHEA, testosterone, progesterone, estrogen, and cortisol. It’s produced mainly in the adrenal glands and brain, and plays a critical role in stress resilience, cognitive function, mood, and overall hormone balance. Low pregnenolone is often seen with burnout, chronic stress, or low DHEA/testosterone—especially if the pituitary signals look fine but downstream hormones are low.

data.name: AST
data.description: AST (Aspartate Aminotransferase) is an enzyme found in your liver, heart, and muscles. It’s released into the blood when cells in these tissues are stressed or damaged. While often used to assess liver health, elevated AST can also reflect muscle strain, overtraining, or even cardiovascular stress. Best interpreted alongside ALT to differentiate between liver and muscle-related causes. Useful for tracking inflammation, recovery, and overall tissue stress.

data.name: Renal Panel (10)
data.description: The renal panel tracks kidney function, electrolyte balance, and fluid regulation—essential for recovery, detox, blood pressure, and performance under physical stress. It includes markers like BUN, creatinine, eGFR, sodium, potassium, chloride, CO₂, calcium, phosphorus, and glucose. This panel helps you spot early signs of dehydration, overtraining, poor recovery, or metabolic dysfunction before they become problems.

data.name: Vitamin D
data.description: 25-Hydroxyvitamin D is the main circulating form of vitamin D and the best marker of your overall vitamin D status. It supports immune health, hormone balance, mood, bone density, and inflammation control. Low levels are common—especially in winter, darker climates, or high-stress states—and can wreck energy, immune function, and recovery.

data.name: Creatine Kinase-MB Fraction(CKMB)
data.description: A creatine kinase (CK) lab test measures the total amount of creatine kinase enzyme in the blood, which is crucial for energy production in muscles. Elevated CK levels can indicate muscle damage or stress, as this enzyme is released into the bloodstream when muscle fibers are injured. This test is often used to diagnose conditions such as myocardial infarction (heart attack), muscular dystrophy, and rhabdomyolysis, a severe breakdown of muscle tissue. It can also help monitor muscle damage in athletes or those with muscle-wasting diseases. Abnormal CK levels necessitate further investigation to identify the underlying cause of muscle injury.

data.name: Folate
data.description: Folate (vitamin B9) is crucial for methylation, DNA repair, red blood cell production, and brain function. It works closely with B12 to support energy, mood, and detox. Low folate can cause fatigue, brain fog, poor recovery, or anemia—especially if you’re training hard or under stress. Active or “methylated” folate (5-MTHF) is the form your body actually uses, especially important if you have MTHFR variants.

data.name: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT), Free — LC/MS/Dialysis
data.description: This test measures free (bioavailable) DHT using LC/MS (liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry) with equilibrium dialysis — the gold standard for hormone testing. It gives you a precise read on the active, unbound form of dihydrotestosterone, a potent testosterone metabolite that drives libido, muscle density, confidence, and energy. Free DHT is the best way to assess how much androgenic activity is actually hitting your receptors, especially if total DHT or testosterone looks normal but symptoms are off.

data.name: Free T3
data.description: Free T3 is the active thyroid hormone—the one that actually hits your cells and turns up metabolism, energy, fat-burning, and brain function. It’s converted from T4 and is far more powerful. Low Free T3 is one of the most common patterns behind fatigue, weight gain, brain fog, and cold intolerance, especially in high-stress or under-recovery states. It’s your real-world metabolic throttle.

data.name: Fasting Insulin
data.description: Fasting insulin measures how much insulin your body needs to keep blood sugar stable when you haven’t eaten. It’s one of the best early indicators of insulin resistance—long before glucose or A1c go bad. High insulin means your cells aren’t responding well, which can wreck fat loss, energy, and long-term health. Low, steady insulin suggests efficient fuel use, fat adaptation, and metabolic flexibility.

data.name: Lipoprotein(a)
data.description: Lipoprotein(a) is a genetically driven cholesterol particle that behaves a lot like LDL, but with added stickiness. It increases the risk of atherosclerosis, blood clots, and heart disease, especially when paired with other lipids like high ApoB or low HDL. You can’t lower it much with lifestyle alone, which makes it a powerful long-term risk marker. If your Lp(a) is high, the strategy becomes reducing inflammation, oxidative stress, and overall ApoB particle burden.

data.name: Triiodothyronine (T3)
data.description: T3 is your active thyroid hormone—it drives metabolism, body temperature, energy, and even mood. It’s more potent than T4, and when T3 is low, everything can feel sluggish. When it’s high, things speed up: metabolism, energy, even anxiety.

data.name: Iron
data.description: Serum Iron measures how much iron is circulating in your blood right now. It's a snapshot—not stored iron, but what's available for use. Levels can swing based on time of day, inflammation, or recent meals, so it’s best interpreted alongside ferritin, UIBC, and iron saturation. Crucial for energy, oxygen transport, and brain function.

data.name: Triglyceride
data.description: Triglycerides are fats floating in your blood—your body’s way of storing excess energy. High levels usually mean you’re overeating carbs or not burning enough energy. They’re a key marker of metabolic health and insulin sensitivity. Lower levels mean cleaner blood flow and better fat-burning efficiency.

data.name: Estradiol, Ultrasensitive, LC/MS
data.description: Estradiol (E2) is the most potent form of estrogen. In men, it’s made mostly by converting testosterone via aromatase. While often labeled a “female hormone,” estradiol is essential for libido, brain function, mood, bone health, and keeping your testosterone in balance. Too little = stiff joints, mood swings, poor libido. Too much = water retention, gynecomastia, irritability. The sensitive assay gives an accurate read in men (standard assays often overestimate).

data.name: Anemia Profile B
data.description: This panel checks for the most common nutrient and blood-based causes of fatigue, low energy, and poor oxygen delivery. It includes iron markers, B12, folate, and red blood cell metrics—giving you a full picture of how well your body is building and fueling red blood cells. It’s a go-to panel if you’re dealing with burnout, low endurance, brain fog, or suspect nutrient deficiencies.

data.name: IGF-1
data.description: IGF-1 is a hormone produced in the liver in response to growth hormone (GH). It drives cell growth, repair, muscle gain, and insulin sensitivity, and plays a big role in recovery, aging, and anabolic signaling. It acts like a middleman between your brain's GH signal and how your tissues respond. Low IGF-1 can reflect under-recovery, stress, low GH output, or aging. Too high may accelerate aging or cancer risk if sustained long-term.

data.name: D-Dimer
data.description: A blood marker that reflects active clot formation and breakdown. Elevated levels suggest increased coagulation activity and are commonly used to help assess clot risk and systemic inflammation. Results are reported as a numeric value, with higher levels indicating greater fibrin turnover.

data.name: Cholesterol in HDL
data.description: HDL is known as the “good” cholesterol because it helps clear excess cholesterol from your bloodstream and arteries, returning it to the liver for processing. Higher HDL is linked to better cardiovascular health, reduced inflammation, and improved metabolic flexibility. It's also involved in hormone transport and antioxidant activity. Raising HDL isn’t just about the number—it’s about improving the quality of your lipid metabolism and overall resilience.

data.name: Magnesium
data.description:
Magnesium is involved in 300+ enzymatic reactions — think energy production, muscle recovery, mood regulation, sleep quality, and blood sugar control. Serum magnesium is what most labs use, but it's a blunt tool — only ~1% of your total magnesium is in the blood, and levels are tightly regulated. So a “normal” value doesn’t always mean optimal.

If you're tracking recovery, sleep, or metabolic flexibility — or supplementing — it's still useful, especially when paired with RBC magnesium or symptom context.

data.name: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
data.description: DHT is a supercharged version of testosterone—it’s stronger, more targeted, and drives things like libido, aggression, skin oil, and strength. High DHT levels can supercharge masculinity, but too much can also trigger acne or hair loss. Low levels often feel like low drive and low edge.

data.name: Ferritin
data.description: Ferritin is your iron storage protein—it’s the best marker for how much iron your body actually has in reserve. Low ferritin can tank your energy, recovery, endurance, and focus—often before hemoglobin or RBC markers crash. High ferritin, on the other hand, may reflect inflammation or iron overload. It’s one of the most critical markers for oxygen delivery, especially if you train hard, fast, or sweat a lot.

data.name: DHEA
data.description: DHEA is an adrenal hormone and precursor to testosterone and estrogen. It plays a big role in energy, mood, libido, immune function, and stress resilience. High DHEA usually signals strong adrenal output and anabolic drive. Low levels can mean chronic stress, burnout, under-recovery, or aging-related hormonal decline. It’s like a battery check for your endocrine system—especially useful if you’re overtraining, cutting, or feeling flat.

data.name: TMAO (Trimethylamine N-oxide)
data.description: TMAO is a compound produced when your gut bacteria metabolize certain nutrients—mostly choline, carnitine, and lecithin—and your liver converts them. Elevated TMAO levels have been linked to cardiovascular risk, inflammation, and metabolic dysfunction, though the research is still evolving. Higher levels often reflect gut microbiome imbalances, excess animal product intake, or impaired renal clearance.

data.name: Albumin
data.description: Albumin is the main protein in your blood, made by the liver. It helps maintain fluid balance, transports hormones and nutrients, and acts as a powerful antioxidant. Optimal levels reflect strong liver function, nutritional status, and systemic stability. Low albumin can be a sign of inflammation, poor protein intake, or chronic stress, while high levels are usually linked to dehydration. A foundational marker for resilience, recovery, and repair.

data.name: Interleukin 6 [Mass/Vol]
data.description: IL-6 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine — a chemical signal your immune system uses during stress, infection, injury, or chronic inflammation. In short bursts, IL-6 is helpful (like post-workout). But when it stays elevated, it’s linked to aging, insulin resistance, mood issues, and poor recovery. It’s one of the most direct markers for silent, chronic inflammation.

data.name: Prostate specific Ag
data.description: PSA is a protein made by the prostate gland. While often used to screen for prostate cancer, elevated levels can also come from inflammation, benign enlargement (BPH), or recent ejaculation or exercise. It’s not a perfect test on its own, but it’s useful as a trend marker—especially if you're over 40 or on testosterone therapy. Sudden spikes or consistently high values should be evaluated further.

data.name: Thyroid Panel With TSH
data.description: This panel measures your brain-thyroid communication and hormone output. It includes TSH (the brain’s signal), Total T4, T3 Uptake, and the Free Thyroxine Index (FTI)—giving you a clear view of thyroid production, hormone transport, and bioavailability. It's useful for spotting early thyroid dysfunction, sluggish metabolism, or hormone-binding issues long before they show up in symptoms.

data.name: Lipid Panel With LDL/HDL Ratio
data.description: This version of the lipid panel includes all standard cholesterol markers—Total Cholesterol, HDL, LDL, VLDL, and Triglycerides—along with the LDL/HDL ratio, a key indicator of lipid balance and cardiovascular risk. The LDL/HDL ratio helps you understand whether your cholesterol transport system is protective or leaning toward plaque buildup. It adds context to your standard lipids, especially when evaluating heart health, inflammation, and metabolic performance.

data.name: CRP (High Sensitivity)
data.description: CRP (High Sensitivity) is a highly sensitive marker of systemic inflammation. It reflects your body’s baseline inflammatory tone—even when you’re not sick or injured. Chronic low-grade inflammation is linked to everything from heart disease to insulin resistance to poor recovery. Elevated CRP doesn't tell you what's wrong, but it tells you that your immune system is on alert. It's one of the most powerful early warning markers for long-term health risk and recovery capacity.

data.name: C-Peptide, Serum
data.description: C-Peptide is a marker of insulin production — it’s released in equal amounts when your pancreas makes insulin. Since insulin is tough to measure accurately due to fluctuations and rapid clearance, C-Peptide gives a cleaner signal of how much your body is working to manage blood sugar. High C-Peptide means your body is pumping out insulin (possible early insulin resistance); low means your pancreas isn’t producing much, which could signal burnout or dysfunction.

data.name: Myeloperoxidase (P) [Moles/Vol]
data.description: MPO is a pro-inflammatory enzyme released by white blood cells during oxidative stress and immune activation. It’s a powerful early warning signal for blood vessel inflammation, oxidative damage, and plaque instability — even before traditional cholesterol markers look bad. Elevated MPO can show up with chronic inflammation, infections, poor recovery, or cardiovascular risk. It’s one of the best early-stage cardiovascular aging markers that most people aren’t watching.

data.name: Magnesium (RBC)
data.description: Magnesium is a foundational mineral for energy, sleep, muscle function, and stress response. RBC Magnesium measures how much is stored inside your red blood cells — not just floating in your blood — making it way more useful for spotting chronic deficiencies. If you’re training hard, under stress, or not sleeping great, low magnesium can quietly wreck your progress.

data.name: Vitamin B7 (Biotin)
data.description:
Biotin (Vitamin B7) is important for turning food into energy and keeping your skin, hair, and nails healthy. Most people get enough biotin from a normal diet, but some can have low levels.
Not having enough biotin can cause hair loss, skin rashes, and brittle nails. It also helps your body process fats and sugars properly.

data.name: Bilirubin
data.description: Bilirubin is a yellow compound made when your body breaks down old red blood cells. It’s processed by the liver, so it’s a key marker for liver function, detox capacity, and oxidative stress. Mildly elevated levels can be harmless (especially in Gilbert’s Syndrome), but significant increases may reflect liver congestion, bile flow issues, or detox stress. It’s also a powerful endogenous antioxidant, so optimal levels may offer protective benefits

data.name: Small LDL-P
data.description: Small LDL-P measures the number of small, dense LDL particles—the kind most likely to cause plaque and inflammation. These are the troublemakers of cholesterol. Even if your total LDL is normal, having a lot of these is a bigger risk factor for heart issues.

data.name: Total Testosterone
data.description: Total testosterone measures the full amount of testosterone in your blood—both bound and free. It’s a good top-level marker of hormonal status, sex drive, energy, strength, and overall vitality. But it doesn’t tell the whole story. A normal total T with low free T can still feel like low testosterone. That’s why context—especially SHBG and free T—is key.

data.name: Calcium
data.description: Calcium isn’t just for bones — it also regulates nerve signals, muscle contraction, heart rhythm, and hormone release. Blood calcium is tightly controlled, so small shifts can flag deeper issues with vitamin D, parathyroid function, magnesium, or kidney health. Most of your calcium is stored in bone — blood calcium reflects your body's moment-to-moment regulation.

data.name: Hepatic Function Panel (7)
data.description: This panel tracks key markers of liver function, detox capacity, and bile flow. It includes enzymes like ALT, AST, ALP, and proteins like albumin, bilirubin, and total protein. Together, these give a full picture of how your liver is handling stress, inflammation, nutrients, alcohol, meds, and metabolic load. If you’re training hard, supplementing aggressively, or dialing in recovery, this panel helps you spot early signs of strain or imbalance.

data.name: Creatine Kinase (CK), Total
data.description: A creatine kinase (CK) lab test measures the total amount of creatine kinase enzyme in the blood, which is crucial for energy production in muscles. Elevated CK levels can indicate muscle damage or stress, as this enzyme is released into the bloodstream when muscle fibers are injured. This test is often used to diagnose conditions such as myocardial infarction (heart attack), muscular dystrophy, and rhabdomyolysis, a severe breakdown of muscle tissue. It can also help monitor muscle damage in athletes or those with muscle-wasting diseases. Abnormal CK levels necessitate further investigation to identify the underlying cause of muscle injury.

data.name: LDL Cholesterol (Direct)
data.description:
Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) represents the amount of cholesterol carried by LDL particles, the primary drivers of cholesterol deposition in arterial walls. Elevated LDL contributes directly to atherosclerotic plaque formation and is a major causal risk factor for cardiovascular disease (ASCVD).

A direct LDL test measures LDL cholesterol without relying on formulas, making it more accurate when triglycerides are elevated, in non-fasting states, or in insulin resistance and metabolic syndrome.

data.name: T4, Free (Direct)
data.description: Free T4 measures the amount of unbound thyroxine (T4) circulating in your blood—the form that’s available to convert into active T3. It reflects how well your thyroid is producing hormone, and how much is actually available for metabolic use. It’s more meaningful than Total T4 because it excludes the portion that’s bound to proteins and inactive. Free T4 is especially useful alongside TSH and Free T3 to assess thyroid function, conversion efficiency, and energy regulation.

data.name: Prolactin
data.description: Prolactin is a sneaky disruptor of performance, sex drive, and cycle health. It is best known for its role in breastfeeding, but it also regulates dopamine, mood, libido, and hormone signaling. In men and non-lactating women, high prolactin usually signals stress, low dopamine, or hormone imbalance. Elevated prolactin can suppress testosterone, lower libido, impair ovulation, and cause brain fog or emotional flatness.

data.name: FSH
data.description: FSH is a pituitary hormone that tells your body to produce sex hormones—like testosterone and estrogen—and helps regulate reproductive function. In men, FSH supports sperm production. In women, it triggers egg development and ovulation. Low FSH may reflect pituitary suppression from stress, overtraining, or high estrogen. High FSH can signal poor feedback from the ovaries/testes—often due to menopause, low gonadal function, or PCOS compensation.

data.name: Apolipoprotein A-1
data.description: ApoA1 is the main protein in HDL (the “good” cholesterol) and plays a key role in clearing cholesterol from your arteries. It helps shuttle cholesterol back to the liver for recycling or disposal—a process called reverse cholesterol transport. Higher ApoA1 means better cardiovascular protection, improved lipid balance, and potentially lower inflammation. It's more predictive than HDL alone, especially in people with metabolic dysfunction.

data.name: CK, Total+Isoenzymes, Serum
data.description: This panel measures total creatine kinase (CK) levels in your blood—along with its key isoenzymes: CK-MM (muscle), CK-MB (heart), and CK-BB (brain/gut). It gives you a full picture of where your body might be experiencing stress, damage, or recovery demands—whether from intense training, inflammation, or internal strain. Great for spotting overtraining, muscle breakdown, cardiac stress, or neurological impact depending on which CK type is elevated.

data.name: Lipid Panel w/ Chol/HDL Ratio
data.description: The Total Cholesterol to HDL ratio is a simple but powerful metric used to estimate cardiovascular risk. It reflects the balance between all cholesterol in the blood and the “good” HDL cholesterol that helps clear it out. A lower ratio is generally better, indicating more protective HDL relative to total cholesterol. This ratio helps identify lipid-related risk even when other numbers seem normal, making it valuable for tracking heart health, fat metabolism, and long-term resilience.

labOptions.biomarkerName: Lipid Panel w/ Chol/HDL Ratio - LabCorp

data.name: Iron and TIBC
data.description: These two markers show how much iron is available in your blood and how well your body can transport it. Serum iron tells you what’s circulating right now, while TIBC reflects how much more iron your system could carry. Together, they help you spot iron deficiency, inflammation, or overload—key factors for energy, endurance, brain function, and recovery.

data.name: Free Testosterone
data.description: Free testosterone is the active, unbound form of testosterone—the portion not tied up by SHBG or albumin. This is what actually interacts with androgen receptors and drives results: libido, muscle retention, motivation, energy, and recovery. You can have “normal” total T but feel off if your free T is low. It’s one of the most important markers for androgen status and performance.

data.name: Lipid Panel
data.description: The Lipid Panel measures key markers related to fat metabolism, cardiovascular risk, and hormonal health—including Total Cholesterol, HDL, LDL, VLDL, and Triglycerides. This panel helps assess how well your body is transporting and managing fats, and whether you’re storing, burning, or overloading them. It's essential for tracking inflammation, metabolic flexibility, energy balance, and long-term cardiovascular health.

data.name: FSH and LH
data.description: This panel measures FSH (Follicle-Stimulating Hormone) and LH (Luteinizing Hormone) — the two key pituitary signals that regulate your sex hormone production. Together, they control testosterone in men and estrogen, ovulation, and cycle regularity in women. These hormones also reflect deeper stress and recovery status, since they’re easily disrupted by overtraining, under-eating, or hormonal imbalances.

data.name: Rheumatoid factor Qn
data.description:
Rheumatoid Factor is an autoantibody — it shows up when your immune system starts attacking healthy tissue, especially in joints. It’s most often associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis, but elevated RF can also show up in other autoimmune conditions or even chronic infections. High doesn’t always mean disease, but it does mean your immune system is more activated than it should be.

If you're dealing with joint stiffness, pain, or fatigue, RF is a key clue — but should always be interpreted alongside symptoms and other markers (like CRP, ESR, or anti-CCP).

data.name: Thyroglobulin Antibody
data.description:
Thyroglobulin antibodies (TgAb) are part of the body’s immune response against your thyroid. High levels suggest the immune system is mistaking thyroid tissue for a threat, which can contribute to autoimmune thyroid conditions like Hashimoto’s or, less commonly, Graves’. It doesn’t tell you how well your thyroid is working directly — but it does flag inflammation or potential damage to your thyroid gland.

If you're tracking thyroid symptoms (fatigue, weight gain, brain fog, cold sensitivity), this marker helps detect root-level immune stress.

data.name: NMR LipoProfile+Lipids+IR+Gph
data.description: This advanced panel combines a traditional lipid profile with NMR particle testing, insulin resistance markers, and glycophospholipid (Gph) data. It gives a detailed look at the size, number, and quality of cholesterol particles—not just how much cholesterol is present. Paired with insulin resistance and glycation markers, this panel uncovers early signs of metabolic dysfunction, cardiovascular risk, and inflammation—often before standard labs show problems. Ideal for tracking lipid particle health, metabolic efficiency, and disease prevention strategies.

data.name: Amenorrhea Profile
data.description: This panel looks at key hormones involved in menstrual cycle regulation to figure out why your period has stopped or become irregular. It checks for issues with brain-to-ovary signaling, stress, thyroid dysfunction, or conditions like PCOS. Useful for spotting the effects of overtraining, under-eating, or hormonal imbalances before they cause bigger issues with energy, mood, or metabolism.

data.name: Thyroxine (T4)
data.description: Total T4 measures the full amount of thyroxine in your blood—both bound and unbound. T4 is the main hormone produced by your thyroid and acts as the precursor to T3, the active form. Most of it is bound to transport proteins and inactive, so while it gives you a good sense of production, it doesn’t reflect actual activity without looking at T3, T3 Uptake, or Free T4. Still, it’s a valuable marker for thyroid output and upstream hormone availability.

data.name: Somatotropin (Growth Hormone)
data.description: Somatotropin is growth hormone, the signal that drives muscle development, fat burning, recovery, and even anti-aging repair. It’s released in pulses, mostly during deep sleep, fasting, and intense training. Blood GH isn’t always the best way to measure long-term output (IGF-1 is more stable), but elevated or deficient values can give important clues. Think of it like your body's in-house "rebuild and renew" hormone.

data.name: Leptin
data.description: Leptin is your body’s “fullness signal” — made by fat cells to tell your brain you have enough energy stored. When leptin is working, it curbs hunger and boosts metabolism. But if levels stay elevated, your brain can become leptin-resistant — you feel hungrier, metabolism slows, and it’s harder to lose weight. Think of leptin as your long-term energy thermostat — key for fat loss, energy regulation, and hormonal balance.

data.name: Lactate
data.description: Lactate is a byproduct of your metabolism — it rises when your body shifts into anaerobic mode (think sprinting, intense lifting, or stress). While it’s often seen as a fatigue marker, lactate is also recycled as fuel, especially by the brain and heart. Chronically elevated levels can suggest overtraining, poor mitochondrial function, hypoxia, or metabolic dysfunction. Used correctly, it's a powerful marker of cellular efficiency and recovery status.

data.name: Basic Metabolic Panel (8)
data.description: The BMP checks core blood chemistry markers that reflect hydration, electrolytes, kidney function, blood sugar, and acid-base balance. It’s a fast, high-leverage snapshot of how your body is handling stress, recovery, and fuel. This panel is foundational—especially for tracking training load, metabolic health, and recovery status.

data.name: Advanced Lipid Panel, Cardio IQ
data.description: The Advanced Lipid Panel (Cardio IQ) goes far beyond a standard cholesterol test to give a deeper look at your heart health. It measures not just total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides, but also how many cholesterol particles you have, their size, and whether they’re the more dangerous types linked to plaque buildup. It also includes key markers like ApoB and Lipoprotein(a), which can reveal hidden cardiovascular risk even when basic cholesterol looks “normal.” This test is ideal if you want a more precise, data-driven view of heart disease risk and how your body is actually handling fats in the blood.

labOptions.biomarkerName: Advanced Lipid Panel, Cardio IQ - Bioreference

data.name: Cystatin C
data.description: Cystatin C is a protein made by all cells and filtered by your kidneys—making it a highly sensitive marker for kidney function and early-stage decline. Unlike creatinine, it’s less affected by muscle mass, so it's often more accurate for biohackers, athletes, and lean individuals. Elevated levels may point to reduced filtration, chronic inflammation, or cardiovascular risk, even when other kidney markers look normal. Great for tracking cellular cleanup, filtration efficiency, and longevity risk.

data.name: Electrolyte Panel
data.description: This panel measures your core electrolytes—sodium, potassium, chloride, and CO₂ (bicarbonate)—which regulate hydration, nerve signaling, muscle contraction, acid-base balance, and overall energy. These markers shift fast under stress, training, sauna use, or dietary extremes (like low-carb or fasting). It’s one of the most underrated tools for tracking how well your system is managing fluid balance, mineral intake, and recovery.

data.name: GlycA
data.description: GlycA is a high-sensitivity marker of chronic inflammation, measuring glycosylated proteins linked to your immune response. Unlike CRP, which can spike from short-term illness or workouts, GlycA reflects long-term, low-grade inflammation—the kind tied to insulin resistance, cardiovascular disease, and biological aging. It's a powerful metric for tracking how your lifestyle, training, or recovery strategies are impacting deep cellular health and inflammatory load.

data.name: Apolipoprotein B
data.description: ApoB is the protein found on all atherogenic lipoproteins—like LDL, VLDL, IDL, and Lp(a). Each of these particles carries one ApoB, so ApoB = the total number of “bad” cholesterol particles. It’s more precise than just measuring LDL cholesterol, especially if your LDL looks "normal" but particle count is high. Elevated ApoB means more cholesterol-carrying particles capable of penetrating artery walls and forming plaque.

data.name: Prolactin [Mass/volume] in Serum or Plasma by Immunoassay
data.description: Prolactin is a sneaky disruptor of performance, sex drive, and cycle health. It is best known for its role in breastfeeding, but it also regulates dopamine, mood, libido, and hormone signaling. In men and non-lactating women, high prolactin usually signals stress, low dopamine, or hormone imbalance. Elevated prolactin can suppress testosterone, lower libido, impair ovulation, and cause brain fog or emotional flatness.

labOptions.biomarkerName: Prolactin [Mass/volume] in Serum or Plasma by Immunoassay - Bioreference

data.name: Iodine [Mass/Vol]
data.description: Iodine is essential for building thyroid hormones — it's literally the “I” in T3 and T4. Low iodine means your thyroid struggles to function, leading to fatigue, cold intolerance, brain fog, and weight gain. On the flip side, too much iodine (especially in supplement form) can disrupt thyroid function, especially in those with autoimmune tendencies like Hashimoto’s.

data.name: Estradiol
data.description: Estradiol (E2) is the most potent form of estrogen. In men, it’s made mostly by converting testosterone via aromatase. While often labeled a “female hormone,” estradiol is essential for libido, brain function, mood, bone health, and keeping your testosterone in balance. Too little = stiff joints, mood swings, poor libido. Too much = water retention, gynecomastia, irritability. The is the standard assay testing and caps the value at 30

data.name: ALT
data.description: ALT is a liver-specific enzyme that rises when liver cells are stressed, inflamed, or damaged. It’s one of the most sensitive markers for liver function and detox capacity. Elevated ALT may reflect poor detox, fatty liver, overtraining, or inflammation from alcohol, medications, or diet. Lower levels are generally a good sign, especially when paired with a healthy AST/ALT ratio. A key marker for anyone focused on longevity, metabolic health, or recovery.

data.name: T3.reverse
data.description: Reverse T3 is the brake pedal of your thyroid system. Instead of activating your metabolism like Free T3, rT3 blocks it. Your body makes more reverse T3 when you're stressed, inflamed, sick, or under-eating — it's a survival move that slows everything down. High rT3 with normal TSH and Free T4 often means you’re converting thyroid hormone inefficiently, leading to fatigue, brain fog, or weight plateaus even when other labs look "fine."

data.name: CBC with Differential/Platelet
data.description: This is an expanded version of the standard CBC. It measures red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets, and breaks down each type of white blood cell (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils). It gives you a clearer view of immune balance, inflammation, recovery, infection status, and nutrient deficiencies. The platelet count also helps track clotting ability and bone marrow activity.

data.name: Advanced Testosterone Panel (Free + Total, LC/MS-MS)
data.description: This is a high-accuracy testosterone panel using equilibrium ultrafiltration and LC/MS-MS — the gold standard for measuring both free and total testosterone. Total T reflects your overall hormone production, while free T shows what’s actually available and active. Together, they give a complete picture of androgen status, anabolic drive, and hormone bioavailability. Especially useful for optimizing performance, identifying low-T symptoms, or fine-tuning TRT protocols.

labOptions.biomarkerName: Advanced Testosterone Panel (Free + Total, LC/MS-MS) - LabCorp

data.name: Cholesterol
data.description: Total cholesterol includes LDL, HDL, and VLDL—it’s a rough snapshot of all the cholesterol-based particles moving through your blood. While it’s often overhyped on its own, context matters. A high number isn’t automatically bad if HDL is strong and triglycerides are low.

data.name: TSH + Free T4
data.description: This panel measures thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (Free T4), giving you a snapshot of how your brain and thyroid are communicating. TSH shows how much your brain is signaling for thyroid hormone, while Free T4 reflects how much hormone is actually available in circulation. Together, they help identify issues like sluggish metabolism, fatigue, weight changes, or mood swings—long before symptoms become chronic.

data.name: TSH
data.description: TSH is the brain’s signal to your thyroid—telling it how hard to work. Higher TSH means your brain is yelling at the thyroid to produce more hormone (often due to sluggish output), while low TSH means your thyroid is either working well or being over-stimulated. TSH is a sensitive marker of thyroid health, but it’s not the full story without Free T4 and Free T3. Even if it’s “normal,” being above 2.5 can reflect early signs of low thyroid function—especially if energy, mood, or metabolism feel off.

data.name: Eosinophils
data.description: Eosinophils are immune cells that deal with parasites, allergic reactions, and chronic inflammation—especially in the gut, skin, or lungs. Elevated levels often point to allergy issues, histamine sensitivity, or immune reactions to food or environment. Tracking eosinophils is a subtle way to spot immune overactivation or inflammation, especially if you’re dealing with fatigue, bloating, skin issues, or asthma-like symptoms.

data.name: NMR LipoProfile+Lipids+IR
data.description: This panel goes way beyond basic cholesterol numbers. It uses NMR (nuclear magnetic resonance) to break down your lipoprotein particles, giving you deeper insight into your cardiovascular and metabolic health—including early insulin resistance.

data.name: PSA Total
data.description: PSA is a protein made by the prostate gland. While often used to screen for prostate cancer, elevated levels can also come from inflammation, benign enlargement (BPH), or recent ejaculation or exercise. It’s not a perfect test on its own, but it’s useful as a trend marker—especially if you're over 40 or on testosterone therapy. Sudden spikes or consistently high values should be evaluated further.
